summary: Defines how IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies are carried over FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network. It is a standards-track document describing the encapsulation used on those networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers on a fiber ring need an agreed way to put their messages into the ring. This rule says how to pack Internet messages for it.

questions: how is ip sent over fddi
how does arp work on fddi
subtitle: How IP datagrams and ARP messages are wrapped for travel over FDDI fiber-ring networks.

tldr.problem: Hosts on a Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) ring needed one agreed way to carry IP datagrams and ARP messages so that different vendors' equipment could interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP are wrapped in 802.2 LLC and SNAP headers (8 octets in total), ARP maps 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses, and the MTU is fixed at 4352 octets.
tldr.outcome: It became a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1103, and it covers single MAC stations only; dual MAC stations were left to a future document.

today: RFC 1188 is listed as a Draft Standard and obsoletes RFC 1103; the metadata records no later RFC replacing it. It covers single MAC stations only.

sections.title: Why IP Needs a Rule for FDDI
sections.content:
RFC 1188 aims at compatible, interoperable implementations for sending IP datagrams and ARP requests and replies over FDDI (Fiber Distributed Data Interface). The FDDI standards provide the Physical Layer and the Media Access Control (MAC) sublayer of the Data Link Layer. The rest of the Data Link service comes from the IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) service.

The stack is therefore IP/ARP on top of 802.2 LLC, on top of the FDDI MAC, PHY and PMD, with Station Management (SMT) alongside. The memo borrows heavily from RFC 1042, the equivalent rule for IEEE 802 networks, and it obsoletes RFC 1103.

The scope is limited: it describes single MAC stations (single-attach or dual-attach). Operation on dual MAC stations is left to a forthcoming document.
sections.plainLanguage: A fiber ring is a road, and IP is the cargo. This document is the shipping rule for putting the cargo on that road.

sections.title: The LLC and SNAP Encapsulation
sections.content:
IP datagrams and ARP messages must be encapsulated in 802.2 LLC and the Sub-Network Access Protocol (SNAP), inside the FDDI MAC frame. Only LLC Type 1 is used: every frame is a standard Unnumbered Information frame.

The header has fixed values. The DSAP and SSAP are both 170 (the SAP assigned to SNAP) and the control field is 3 (Unnumbered Information). The 24-bit Organization Code in the SNAP header is zero, and the remaining 16 bits carry the EtherType: 2048 for IP and 2054 for ARP. LLC plus SNAP together take 8 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message gets the same small label on the front saying what kind of message it is: one label for IP and one for ARP.

sections.title: Address Resolution with ARP
sections.content:
The mapping from 32-bit Internet addresses to 48-bit FDDI addresses is done with the dynamic discovery procedure of ARP (RFC 826). Each host must know its own Internet address, answer ARP requests properly, and use ARP to translate addresses when needed.

The ARP parameters are fixed: protocol type 2048 for IP, hardware address length 6, protocol address length 4, and operation code 1 for request and 2 for reply.

The hardware type needs care. IEEE 802 networks use code 6 and Ethernet uses 1, and the mismatch causes trouble in bridged setups. To stay interoperable with Ethernet, ARP packets shall be sent with hardware type 1 and shall be accepted with either 1 or 6.

Hardware addresses inside ARP packets must be in canonical bit order, with the Group bit as the low-order bit of the first octet. FDDI normally writes addresses with the Group bit in the high-order position, so the bits are reversed within each octet.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP is like shouting on the ring, who has this Internet address? The owner answers with its hardware address. The document fixes the exact wording of the shout so everybody understands it.

sections.title: Broadcast, Multicast and Byte Order
sections.content:
The IP broadcast address (host part all binary ones) must map to the FDDI broadcast address of all binary ones. Multicast follows the method in RFC 1112, which must be used if IP multicasting is supported: the low-order 23 bits of the IP address are placed in the low-order 23 bits of the group address 01-00-5E-00-00-00. For example, 224.255.0.2 maps to 01-00-5E-7F-00-02. In native (bit-reversed) order on the wire that becomes 80-00-7A-FE-00-40.

Hosts directly connected to FDDI networks shall not use the trailer encapsulation that some Unix 4.x bsd versions use. IP datagrams travel as a series of 8-bit bytes in big-endian order.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting to everyone and shouting to a chosen group both need special mailbox names. The rule gives a simple recipe for building those names from the Internet address.

sections.title: Packet Size and MAC Layer Details
sections.content:
The FDDI MAC defines a maximum frame of 9000 symbols (4500 octets), which leaves roughly 4470 octets for data after the LLC/SNAP header. To leave room for future extensions to the MAC header and frame status, the MTU is set to 4352 octets: 4096 octets of data and 256 octets of network-layer and higher headers. Implementations must not send packets larger than the MTU.

Gateways must accept packets up to the MTU and fragment them when needed. Hosts must be ready to accept packets up to the MTU, but must not send datagrams longer than 576 octets unless they know the destination will accept them. There is no minimum packet size, and implementations must be ready to receive and ignore trailing pad octets.

Only 48-bit addresses are used with IP and ARP. All IP and ARP frames are sent as Asynchronous LLC frames using Unrestricted tokens, and the priority is a local matter that should be tunable. The Frame Copied (C) and Address Recognized (A) indicators may be used as the implementation chooses, but the RFC notes that their meaning in the presence of bridges was not well defined at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: A truck on this road can carry a big load, but the rule sets a safe limit a bit below the maximum. Smaller loads are still sent when the destination is far away.

sections.title: IEEE 802.2 Requirements
sections.content:
To comply with 802.2, every implementation must support Class I service, which needs Unnumbered Information (UI), XID and TEST frames. Stations need not be able to send XID and TEST commands, but must be able to send responses. UI responses and UI commands with the Poll bit set are ignored, and UI commands whose DSAP or SSAP is not the SNAP SAP are not processed as IP or ARP.

XID and TEST commands must be answered only when the DSAP is the SNAP SAP (170), the Null SAP (0) or the Global SAP (255). The response copies the command's SSAP into its DSAP, and the Final bit copies the command's Poll bit. An XID response carries the information field 129.1.0 (Class I, connectionless), and a TEST response echoes the command's information field.
sections.plainLanguage: Stations must also reply politely when another station asks are you there? or who are you? These replies keep the ring friendly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It defines framing and address mapping and makes no security claims.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not talk about keeping messages secret or safe. It only covers how to pack and address them.
